title: Store scan times on the warehouse's clock

blocks.text: Each warehouse has a legacy table with a `TIMESTAMP` column (no zone) for the time a parcel was scanned. The warehouse staff read that column directly, so it must show what the clocks in the warehouse showed at the scan. The old DAO takes and returns `java.sql.Timestamp`, and writes the date and time a `Timestamp` gives through `toLocalDateTime()`. The new scanning service, written with `java.time`, runs on servers whose default zone nobody controls, and it serves warehouses in several zones.
Finish the two `TODO` methods in `src/main/java/practice/ScanTimeColumn.java`. Each `ScanTimeColumn` is built with its warehouse's zone:

items: `toColumn(scanned)`: the value to hand the DAO for a scan at that moment;
`fromColumn(column)`: the moment of the scan that a row read by the DAO records.

blocks.text: The tests use warehouses in two zones and never change the JVM's default zone. About two lines in total.

cases.says: two scans ninety minutes apart are stored as values ninety minutes apart
two rows ninety minutes apart read as moments ninety minutes apart
the stored date and time are what the warehouse's clocks showed at the scan, for warehouses in two zones
a row reads as the moment its date and time stand for on the warehouse's clock, for warehouses in two zones

origin.section: Timestamp and java.sql.Date Turn Local Values into Moments in the JVM's Default Zone

concepts: from/toInstant carry a moment and valueOf/toLocalDateTime a wall-clock value; a wall-clock column in a known zone is converted with that zone in java.time before valueOf.
Timestamp.valueOf, toLocalDateTime, java.sql.Date.valueOf and toLocalDate convert through the JVM's default zone, so the same values give different moments or dates under different default zones.
